newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin still coy on French deficit -economists.
newsitem.headline: Jospin still coy on French deficit -economists.

text.p: Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin gave few clues during a television appearance on Thursday about France's budget deficit in 1997, the crucial qualifying year for a single currency, economists said on Friday.
But they said he appeared to be rowing back on some of the Socialist's Party's hardline policies announced during the election campaign which brought it to power last month, ousting the centre-right.

"Pragmatism was the main feature of the prime minister's speech," said Joanne Perez at Merrill Lynch. "We had confirmation of a softening of the Keynsian approach the new government started out with."
Economists praised Jospin's willingness to consider privatising some state-owned companies and his go-slow approach to job creation after the party's campaign promise to generate 700,000 new jobs.
They said Jospin, interviewed by France 2, appeared to have ruled out an expansionist economic policy in the run-up to monetary union.
"His margins for manoeuvre are very limited," said Vincent Chaigneau of Societe Generale. "We're not going to see an expansionist policy. He was preparing the terrain."
While Jospin admitted the need to curb spending, economists were unhappy over his vagueness over how much he would rein in the public deficit to meet terms for a single currency.
They were also worried by his hints at tax increases.

"Jospin didn't give any hints about his fiscal targets in 1997," said Eric Chaney of Morgan Stanley. "Does he want the budget deficit to be significantly below 3.5 percent (of GDP)? And if corrective measures are taken, what kind of measures would they be? I had the impression they would be higher taxes."
Analysts have said this year's public deficit could be between 3.4 percent and 3.8 percent of GDP, and have forecast that the government would try to reduce it to 3.3 percent.

But even that would leave France at odds with Germany, its main partner in monetary union, which is aiming for exactly 3.0 percent of GDP to comply with a strict reading of the Maastricht treaty on the single currency.

Jospin reiterated his commitment to the single European currency. At the same time, he said he could not take economic measures that would hit growth and pledged to take account of French opinion in setting policies.
An aide said on Friday Jospin had meant he would "sound out" voters through "direct contact" -- via unions, polls, the media -- and not through a referendum as some commentators had wondered.

In his clearest statement so far on state sell-offs, Jospin said he would look at privatisation on a case-by-case basis, seeking the "best solutions" and would not be guided by national interest, not ideology.
"It's clear he wants to get rid of all those firms nationalised at the start of the Socialist era (in the 1980s)," said Chaney.
"I think the government will eventually privatise GAN, CIC, Thomson-CSF, Credit Lyonnais," Chaney said.
Financial markets showed no reaction to Jospin's remarks, partly, analysts said, because they contained no significant negative surprises.
